questions.q: What decides which records are even eligible to be submitted into an approval process?
questions.explain: Entry Criteria is the filter (similar to a report filter) that determines which records can enter the approval process at all.

questions.q: What commonly happens to a record while it is actively in an approval process?
options: It is automatically deleted if not approved within 24 hours
It is locked, preventing further edits until approved, rejected, or recalled
It becomes visible only to System Administrators
Its validation rules are automatically disabled
questions.explain: Initial submission actions typically lock the record, and it stays locked until the process resolves or an admin recalls it.

questions.q: Why would a record-triggered Flow call a Submit for Approval action instead of relying solely on the approval process's own entry criteria?
options: Submit for Approval is required by Salesforce on every approval process
Entry criteria can't reference any fields at all
Approval processes can no longer be created declaratively
Flow can evaluate more complex logic — like a rolling total across other records — that a single static entry-criteria filter can't express
questions.explain: A Flow can loop, call subflows, and evaluate multi-record logic before deciding to submit — something a one-shot entry-criteria filter can't do on its own.

questions.q: Which Flow type is designed to run automatically whenever a record is created, updated, or deleted?
questions.explain: A record-triggered Flow fires automatically on the record DML event itself, and is the modern replacement for most Workflow Rule and Process Builder use cases.

questions.q: A requirement states: 'A specific named manager must explicitly approve every expense report over $5,000, and the approval history must be visible on the record.' Which tool is the better native fit?
questions.explain: Named human sign-off with built-in locking and a visible Approval History is exactly what the approval process is purpose-built for.
